title: The founder who left and the students who came in his place. September 9, 2026.
excerpt: From a Chandigarh-born engineer who sold Hotmail for $400 million to a university that took two decades to build after its founder died, September 9 was a day about the gap between starting something and seeing it finished.
bodyHtml:
Some days this project covers five completely unrelated stories. September 9 wasn't quite that - underneath the space race and the remittance numbers, there was a quieter thread: almost nothing here got finished by the person who started it. The founder who leaves before the payoff. The builder who dies before the institution he imagined actually opens. That gap between starting and finishing turned out to be the real subject of the day.

The email service nobody in India remembers building

Start with Sabeer Bhatia. Born in Chandigarh, he left for engineering studies at Caltech and Stanford, and in 1996, with co-founder Jack Smith, launched Hotmail - one of the first free, web-based email services anyone could simply sign up for. It grew fast enough that Microsoft came calling within two years. On December 30, 1997, Bhatia sold the company for $400 million in stock, a landmark deal for an Indian-origin founder building an American company from scratch.

Almost thirty years later, that deal reads less like a one-off and more like a template. Millions of Indians have since built careers, companies and inventions abroad - success that was never really separate from India's own growth story, just deferred. Increasingly, it flows back as capital and expertise, not just headlines about someone else's exit.

The university that opened twenty-two years after the idea

Then there's Aligarh Muslim University, which became a university on this exact date in a very literal sense. In 1875, Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College on a specific bet: that Muslims in India needed modern, Western-style education without giving up their own identity. He died in 1898, twenty-two years before that bet paid off - it took the Muslim University Association, founded around 1900, another two decades of fundraising and organizing before an Act of the legislature finally converted the college into a university on September 9, 1920.

Sir Syed never saw the university that carries his idea forward. That's not a footnote - it's close to the actual mechanism by which institutions get built. Someone commits to something they will not personally see finished, and the people who come after either honor that bet or let it die. AMU is proof the bet can still pay off, even on a two-decade delay.

The rocket company that didn't wait for permission

Skyroot Aerospace's story runs on a shorter clock, but the same logic. Until recently, only one organization launched rockets from India. Skyroot just became the country's first private space-tech unicorn, hitting a $1.1 billion valuation in May 2026 after raising $60 million - bringing its total funding to $160 million. Its rocket, Vikram-1, can carry up to 350 kilograms into low Earth orbit, built entirely by a private Indian company, with a bigger version already planned for 2027. Over 100 authorizations have now been issued to private space companies nationwide, with more than $870 million invested in the sector.

None of that happened because one founder finished the whole job alone - it happened because a regulatory door opened, and enough people walked through it fast enough to turn one company into an industry within a few years.

The money that keeps arriving on its own schedule

Nearly 19 million Indians now work outside India - a number that's nearly tripled since 2000, from 6.6 million. Last year they sent home $135.46 billion in remittances, an all-time high, up 14% from the year before and nearly double what Mexico, the second-highest recipient, brought in. Close to half of that overseas workforce is based in the Gulf, and these inflows now make up over 10% of India's total current account receipts.

It's the least glamorous story of the day and possibly the steadiest one: no single founder, no single deal, just millions of individual decisions to keep sending money home, repeated often enough to become a macroeconomic fact.

The version that never left the ground

And then the smallest story, which ties the day together better than it has any right to: the rocket that reaches orbit was preceded by a hundred versions that never left the ground - none of them were the failure, all of them were the job. Growth doesn't look like progress from the inside. It looks like repeated, unglamorous attempts that nobody outside is watching, run by people who will very often not be the ones who get credit for the eventual launch.

Five stories, one day. None of them are the whole picture on their own - the picture is what they add up to.

On September 9th, a college that started with one man's stubborn idea became a university.
The rocket that reaches orbit was preceded by a hundred versions that never left the ground - none of them were the failure, all of them were the job.
